newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First proposes radical cuts to immigration.
newsitem.headline: NZ First proposes radical cuts to immigration.

text.p: New Zealand First Party leader Winston Peters on Thursday unveiled his party's immigration policy which would see a maximum of just 10,000 permanent residency approvals each year.
In the year to June there were 55,000 approvals for permanent residency.
Peters told a meeting in the Auckland suburb Pakuranga that the 10,000 would include those migrants accepted under family reunion, business investment and the "points" based migration system.
A separate category would be established for humanitarian migrants and refugees.
Other aspects of NZ First's policy included:
* a full-year probationary period before immigrants are granted New Zealand citizenship,
* and development of a population policy clamping down on refugee "scams".
"New Zealand First's immigration policy has one clear aim. It is to ensure that immigration is in New Zealand's best interests and that it is clearly ordered to that end," Peters said.

He accused some immigrants of abusing New Zealand's hospitality. He said there was strong anecdotal evidence to suggest that many recent migrants continued their main business activity back in their own countries after gaining permanent residency.
Peters said New Zealand had neither the social infrastructure nor the balanced economy to support the new arrivals.

"The detrimental effects of unrestrained immigration are obvious. On the economic front, the Reserve Bank has admitted that the building and property boom in Auckland fuelled, indeed created, by migrants, had caused inflation to rise for all of New Zealand," he said.
That had triggered the Reserve Bank's tight monetary policies which had driven up mortgage and business interest rates.
"Immigration alone cannot be entirely blamed for this state of affairs," Peters said.
"But it was, and continues to remain, a major contributing factor to inflation pressures."
Peters said immigration had also led to "clogged" roads, pressure on schools, strain upon social services and, in some areas, a growing resentment at the dramatic change in a community's culture.
Peters' speech was his first on immigration since NZ First shot up in opinion polls earlier this year on the back of promises to "cut immigration to the bone".
